Chain-of-Thought and Compressed Looped Transformers:
A Memory-Budget Separation

Haozhou Zhang Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Statistics Affiliation: University of Idaho Email: zhan3063@vandals.uidaho.edu
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Chain-of-thought prompting and looped Transformers both give a fixed model more test-time computation, but they differ in what they remember. Chain-of-thought stores intermediate state in generated tokens that remain in the context, whereas a looped Transformer carries state through recurrent hidden activations. We argue that this persistent mutable memory is a central resource for test-time reasoning.

We compare three memory regimes, the compressed latent loop, the full sequence-state loop, and the chain-of-thought scratchpad. Our main result shows that a compressed loop is limited by the size of its recurrent state. Running the loop longer adds computation but does not by itself create a growing scratchpad, so a loop with a small recurrent state remains a small-space reasoner even when run for many steps. Under a standard complexity assumption, such loops cannot decide problems that are 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete under logspace reductions, whereas polynomial-length chain-of-thought can.

The separation is specific to compressed loops, as full sequence-state loops carry state at every input position and live in a memory-rich regime closer to explicit scratchpads. Controlled pointer-chasing and associative-recall sweeps illustrate this memory-budget view, with performance sensitive to whether the persistent-state budget matches the task’s working-memory demand.

1 Introduction

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and recurrent-depth Transformers are two ways of giving a fixed model more computation at test time. In CoT, the model writes intermediate state into generated tokens and later reads those tokens back from the context. In a looped Transformer, the model instead reuses a block on hidden activations, carrying intermediate state through the recurrent hidden state. These two mechanisms both add iteration, but they store intermediate information in different places.

This distinction matters for serial reasoning. Li et al. (2024) show that CoT can supply sequential computation, since with enough generated steps constant-depth Transformers simulate increasingly large Boolean circuits, and Merrill and Sabharwal (2024) characterise the polynomial-length scratchpad regime as 𝖯\mathsf{P}. Looped and latent-thought models have also been shown to be powerful, but the strongest formal comparisons usually study memory-rich loops: the recurrent state contains a full hidden sequence, and therefore grows with the input length or with appended scratch positions. In that regime, looped Transformers can act as programmable computers (Giannou et al., 2023), simulate CoT by appending tokens (Saunshi et al., 2025), and in some parallel-evaluable settings outperform explicit token-by-token reasoning (Xu and Sato, 2026).

The question we study is what remains true when the recurrent state is not a full sequence. A loop may be run for many iterations, but if it carries only a small persistent state from one iteration to the next, then recurrence adds time without adding much mutable memory. We therefore separate the amount of computation performed from the amount of state preserved across steps.

Throughout, nn denotes the input length, dd the hidden width, pp the number of bits used to store each activation, ss the number of compressed recurrent slots, TT the number of loop iterations, and ℓ\ell the number of generated CoT tokens. We write MM for the number of persistent mutable bits carried from one reasoning step to the next. With this accounting, a compressed latent loop has M=s​d​pM=s\,d\,p; a sequence-state loop has M=n​d​pM=n\,d\,p, since it stores a hidden vector at every input position; and a CoT scratchpad has M=Θ⁡(ℓ​log⁡|Σ|)M=\Theta(\ell\log|\Sigma|) (Θ⁡(ℓ)\Theta(\ell) for a fixed vocabulary), since generated tokens are appended to the context and re-read later.

Our formal result isolates the compressed-loop regime. Write 𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(f)\mathsf{DSPACE}(f) for the class of languages a deterministic Turing machine decides using O⁡(f)O(f) work space, polylog⁡(n)=(log⁡n)O⁡(1)\mathrm{polylog}(n)=(\log n)^{O(1)}, and 𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)=⋃c≥1𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡((log⁡n)c)\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n)=\bigcup_{c\geq 1}\mathsf{DSPACE}\!\big((\log n)^{c}\big). A compressed loop with ss recurrent slots, width dd, precision pp, and TT iterations is then simulated in

𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n+log⁡T)).\mathsf{DSPACE}\!\big(O(s\,d\,p+\log n+\log T)\big).

The simulation stores the recurrent state, streams over the read-only input whenever attention needs to inspect it, and reuses the same scratch space at each iteration. Thus, if the persistent state is polylogarithmic in the input length and the loop runs for at most quasi-polynomially many steps (so the iteration counter needs only polylogarithmic space), the loop remains a polylogarithmic-space machine.

This gives a conditional separation from CoT in the memory-constrained regime. Assuming the standard but unproven separation 𝖯⊈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{P}\not\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), such compressed loops cannot decide 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete serial tasks, whereas polynomial-length CoT can under standard expressivity results. This separation is specific to the compressed case. Full sequence-state loops carry n​d​pn\,d\,p persistent bits and lie in a different, memory-rich regime, so what the bound isolates is the limited persistent memory rather than recurrence in general.

Concretely, the paper makes the following five contributions:

  • •

    We formalise persistent mutable memory as a resource for comparing CoT, full sequence-state loops, and compressed latent loops.

  • •

    We prove that compressed latent loops are small-space machines: a loop with only a compressed recurrent state can be simulated by storing that state, streaming over the read-only input, and reusing scratch space across iterations.

  • •

    We show why this argument does not extend to full sequence-state loops in the same way. Once the loop carries hidden state at every input position, the corresponding memory budget is linear in the sequence length, placing these models in the memory-rich regime studied by prior looped-Transformer work.

  • •

    We derive a conditional separation between polylogarithmic-memory compressed loops and polynomial-length CoT on serial polynomial-time tasks, assuming polynomial time is not contained in polylogarithmic space.

  • •

    We connect prior memory-token results on Sudoku to the persistent-memory lens as external motivation, and provide two controlled finite-size probes, a pointer-chasing slot sweep and an associative-recall state-size sweep.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews related work, and Section 3 defines the three reasoners and their memory budgets. Section 4 develops the formal separation in three steps: the small-space bound for compressed loops, the sequence-state endpoint, and the separation from CoT, with detailed proofs deferred to Appendices B, C, D and E. Section 5 presents the empirical studies, and Section 6 discusses the scope of the result.

2 Related work

Expressivity of CoT.

Li et al. (2024) show CoT supplies sequential computation. With ℓ\ell generated steps, constant-depth Transformers simulate Boolean circuits of size ℓ\ell. Merrill and Sabharwal (2024) give a length-parameterised characterisation of decoders with scratchpads, identifying the polynomial-step regime with 𝖯\mathsf{P} under their model assumptions, and Amiri et al. (2025) prove lower bounds on the number of CoT steps required in the hard-attention setting. These works identify the CoT scratchpad as a growing computational resource; in our notation this is the endpoint MCoT=Θ⁡(ℓ)M_{\mathrm{CoT}}=\Theta(\ell) for a fixed token alphabet. Yang et al. (2025) instead modify the scratchpad interface, adding a reduction rule that erases intermediate thoughts to achieve space-efficient universal computation; our CoT endpoint is the standard append-only scratchpad, so erasure or reduction occupies a different point on the same memory axis.

Looped and recurrent-depth Transformers.

Giannou et al. (2023) construct looped Transformers as programmable computers whose input acts as both instruction stream and memory. Saunshi et al. (2025) show looped Transformers solve group-composition-style iterative tasks with logarithmically many loops and can simulate CoT using appended scratch positions. Back de Luca and Fountoulakis (2024) construct looped Transformers that simulate classical graph algorithms (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Kosaraju) and, with extra attention heads, are Turing-complete, while Yang et al. (2024) show looped Transformers can emulate iterative learning algorithms with substantially fewer parameters than standard Transformers on data-fitting tasks. These constructions are memory-rich in the sense relevant here: the loop maintains a full sequence state, padding or scratch positions, or graph-interaction state, rather than only a fixed compressed latent vector, which our Proposition 4.3 recovers as the memory-rich endpoint. Merrill and Sabharwal (2025b); Merrill and Sabharwal (2025a) further study depth, padding, and looping as parallelisable forms of test-time compute, with log-depth already adding expressive power for regular languages and graph connectivity, while padding combined with looping yields exact characterisations in threshold-circuit classes.

Memory tokens and the depth-state trade-off.

Sapunov (2026) studies a single-block Universal Transformer with adaptive computation time and a variable number rr of learned memory tokens on Sudoku-Extreme. The reported threshold between zero and eight memory tokens, the plateau, the dilution boundary, and the substitution between memory size and halt depth are suggestive of a persistent-memory effect, and our space-complexity lens predicts such thresholds when the effective working-state demand exceeds the persistent state available to the model. The architecture also carries sequence-state activations, however, so it is not a clean instance of our compressed-loop model, and we treat it as external motivation rather than a diagnostic test of the separation. Lu et al. (2025) analyse the depth-recurrent model of Geiping et al. (2025), finding only marginal gains from added recurrence depth and limited evidence of interpretable latent CoT. Relatedly, Blayney et al. (2026) mechanistically analyse looped-reasoning models, reporting cyclic fixed points and attention stabilisation across recurrences. These works support the view that recurrence can reorganise computation without necessarily increasing the amount of persistent state.

Recall-memory trade-offs in efficient attention.

A separate line of work measures the state needed for associative recall in efficient sequence models. Arora et al. (2024a) introduce multi-query associative recall as a diagnostic for efficient language models and attribute much of the gap between attention and gated-convolution models to recall ability, while Arora et al. (2024b) identify a recall-throughput trade-off in which fixed-state recurrent alternatives recover recall as the recurrent state or feature dimension grows, at a corresponding memory cost. Okpekpe and Orvieto (2025) further show that the learning rate strongly affects recurrent-model recall, so reported recall gaps partly reflect optimisation. Our associative-recall sweep in Section 5.2 uses this setting as a controlled probe of the same persistent-memory axis; the formal separation concerns compressed looped Transformers and append-only CoT.

CoT versus latent or looped thought.

Xu and Sato (2026) formally compare CoT with latent-thought reasoning, including looped and continuous hidden-state computation, the latter exemplified by the continuous-thought model of Hao et al. (2025). Their results separate the two interfaces along two axes, with latent thought holding an advantage for parallel computation and CoT a separate advantage from stochastic decoding and approximate counting. We study a different axis. Holding attention on deterministic serial computation, we ask what happens when the looped reasoner does not carry a full hidden sequence but only a bounded persistent state; in that memory-constrained regime, the limiting resource is persistent memory rather than parallel depth.

Circuit complexity of Transformers.

Merrill and Sabharwal (2023) place log-precision Transformers in logspace-uniform 𝖳𝖢0\mathsf{TC}^{0}, providing the circuit-complexity background for the comparisons above. We use the same log-precision, logspace-uniform setting to upper-bound compressed latent loops by their persistent mutable memory budget.

3 Models and memory accounting

We now define the three idealised reasoners used in the separation. As above, nn is the input length, dd the hidden width, and pp the number of bits used to store each activation; let ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} denote the pp-bit fixed-point activation set, defined precisely in Appendix A. The memory budget MM counts mutable activation state that persists across reasoning steps; it does not count the fixed parameters, the read-only input x∈Σnx\in\Sigma^{n}, or temporary workspace recomputed within a step. A block BθB_{\theta} is a constant number of multi-head attention and multi-layer-perceptron (MLP) sublayers at precision pp; we assume the log-precision regime p=O⁡(log⁡n)p=O(\log n) and a logspace-uniform parameter family, following Merrill and Sabharwal (2023).

Definition 3.1 (Compressed latent loop CLL⁡[s,d,p,T]\mathrm{CLL}[s,d,p,T]).

The mutable state is zt∈(ℱpd)sz_{t}\in(\mathcal{F}_{p}^{d})^{s}, holding ss persistent slots, initialised by z0=initθ​(x)z_{0}=\mathrm{init}_{\theta}(x), which is either fixed learned memory or computable from the read-only input in O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)O(s\,d\,p+\log n) space. The update

zt+1=Bθ(zt;x),t=0,…,T−1,z_{t+1}=B_{\theta}(z_{t}\,;\,x),\qquad t=0,\dots,T-1,

lets the ss state-slots act as attention queries against the nn read-only input tokens as keys and values. The input side is read-only at every sublayer, where the key and value for input position ii are logspace-computable functions of xix_{i}, the position index, and the parameters, and the block never materialises or updates an nn-position hidden sequence. Only the ss latent slots are mutable across sublayers and iterations; slot-to-slot self-attention among them is permitted, since those slots are already stored in O⁡(s​d​p)O(s\,d\,p) space. The output is decoded from zTz_{T}, and no per-input-token persistent state is carried between iterations. Its persistent memory is MCLL=s​d​pM_{\mathrm{CLL}}=s\,d\,p bits.

Definition 3.2 (Sequence-state loop SSL⁡[d,p,T]\mathrm{SSL}[d,p,T]).

The mutable state is Ht∈(ℱpd)nH_{t}\in(\mathcal{F}_{p}^{d})^{n}, the full length-nn hidden sequence, initialised by H0=embedθ​(x)H_{0}=\mathrm{embed}_{\theta}(x). Each update Ht+1=Bθ​(Ht)H_{t+1}=B_{\theta}(H_{t}) is a full self-attention pass that updates all nn positions, with the input embeddings and positions available as fixed features. This is the standard looped Transformer of Giannou et al. (2023); Saunshi et al. (2025); if padding or scratch positions are appended, they are included in the sequence length nn. Its persistent memory is MSSL=n​d​pM_{\mathrm{SSL}}=n\,d\,p bits.

Definition 3.3 (CoT scratchpad CoT⁡[d,p,ℓ]\mathrm{CoT}[d,p,\ell]).

The model autoregressively emits tokens y1,…,yℓ∈Σy_{1},\dots,y_{\ell}\in\Sigma, each

yt=decode⁡(Bθ​([x;y<t])),y_{t}=\mathrm{decode}\big(B_{\theta}([x\,;\,y_{<t}])\big),

appended to the context and re-read at later steps. Its persistent memory is the scratchpad, MCoT=Θ⁡(ℓ​log⁡|Σ|)M_{\mathrm{CoT}}=\Theta(\ell\log|\Sigma|) bits (Θ⁡(ℓ)\Theta(\ell) for a fixed vocabulary); we count the externally written scratchpad tokens, not implementation-level caches used to accelerate decoding.

For the comparison below, the relevant difference between the three is the persistent mutable memory carried across reasoning steps, fixed by the slot count in a compressed loop, growing with the sequence length in a sequence-state loop, and growing with the scratchpad in chain-of-thought.

4 Space bounds and the memory-budget separation

We prove the separation in three steps: compressed loops admit a small-space simulation; full sequence-state loops instead carry linear state; and combining these with standard chain-of-thought expressivity separates the two in the compressed-memory regime.

4.1 Compressed loops admit a small-space simulation

The memory accounting of Section 3 becomes useful once it is turned into a space simulation. Since a compressed loop carries no mutable state at the input positions, a simulator only needs to store the ss recurrent slots. Attention over the input can be recomputed by streaming over the read-only input tape, and the scratch space can be reused across slots, layers, and iterations. Thus recurrence adds time, but not persistent mutable memory, apart from the counter used to track the loop steps. The full one-block simulation is in Appendix B and the iteration argument in Appendix C.

Lemma 4.1 (One compressed-loop update in small space).

Under the log-precision, logspace-uniform regime, one update z↦Bθ​(z,x)z\mapsto B_{\theta}(z\,;\,x) of a CLL⁡[s,d,p,T]\mathrm{CLL}[s,d,p,T] is computable in deterministic work-space O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)O(s\,d\,p+\log n), given zz stored on the work tape and xx on a read-only input tape.

Proof intuition.

A compressed loop never materialises an nn-position hidden sequence. To update one latent slot, the simulator streams over the read-only input, computing the attention numerator and denominator with a constant number of passes and a few pp-bit registers. Once the slot’s readout has been accumulated, the MLP and residual updates are local computations on O⁡(d​p)O(dp) bits. The same scratch is reused for every slot, so the only persistent workspace is the s​d​ps\,d\,p-bit latent state, plus O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) addressing and arithmetic scratch. Appendix B gives the full finite-precision simulation. ∎

Theorem 4.2 (Compressed loops are space-bounded).

For any CLL⁡[s,d,p,T]\mathrm{CLL}[s,d,p,T] in the log-precision logspace-uniform regime,

CLL⁡[s,d,p,T]⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n+log⁡T)).\mathrm{CLL}[s,d,p,T]\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}\!\big(O(s\,d\,p+\log n+\log T)\big).

In particular, if s​d​p=polylog⁡(n)s\,d\,p=\mathrm{polylog}(n) and log⁡T=polylog⁡(n)\log T=\mathrm{polylog}(n) (e.g. for polynomially many iterations), then CLL⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathrm{CLL}\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n).

The displayed bound assumes O⁡(p)O(p)-space pp-bit arithmetic; under general logspace-uniform arithmetic it carries an additive poly⁡(p)\mathrm{poly}(p) term, still polylogarithmic when p=O⁡(log⁡n)p=O(\log n) (see Appendix A).

Proof intuition.

The simulator runs the loop literally: it stores the current compressed state, computes the next state using Lemma 4.1, overwrites the old state, and advances a log⁡T\log T-bit counter. The input may be rescanned at every iteration, but because it is read-only this increases time, not workspace. Iteration thus adds a counter but no persistent mutable memory. The full proof is in Appendix C. ∎

4.2 The sequence-state endpoint

Section 4.1 bounded compressed loops by the space needed to store their recurrent slots. For sequence-state loops, the same accounting gives a different scale. The recurrent state is the whole hidden sequence: one dd-dimensional pp-bit vector for each of the nn positions, so the persistent state has n​d​pn\,d\,p bits. A simulator can store this sequence and run the same step-by-step argument as before, but the resulting bound is linear in the sequence length. This is the memory-rich regime used by standard looped-Transformer expressivity constructions. Appendix D gives the proof of Proposition 4.3.

Proposition 4.3 (Sequence-state loops are memory-rich).

For SSL⁡[d,p,T]\mathrm{SSL}[d,p,T], the persistent memory is MSSL=n​d​pM_{\mathrm{SSL}}=n\,d\,p, and the simulation argument of Theorem 4.2 gives

SSL⁡[d,p,T]⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(n​d​p+log⁡n+log⁡T)).\mathrm{SSL}[d,p,T]\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(O(n\,d\,p+\log n+\log T)).

For fixed d,pd,p this is Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) space, linear in the sequence length up to the width and precision factors dd and pp. This linear-state endpoint is genuinely memory-rich. The programmable-computer construction of Giannou et al. (2023), combined with the CoT simulation of Saunshi et al. (2025) and the CoT-to-circuits result of Li et al. (2024), places 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete tasks such as the circuit value problem (CVP) within the sequence-state endpoint. Here nn denotes the total sequence length available to the loop, including any padding or dummy scratch positions. Hence, under 𝖯⊈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{P}\not\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), SSL⊈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathrm{SSL}\not\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n).

What separates the two regimes is the scale of the persistent state. Compressed loops keep s​d​ps\,d\,p recurrent bits; sequence-state loops keep n​d​pn\,d\,p recurrent bits. Increasing the number of iterations affects time and adds only the loop counter, while the amount of persistent mutable state is fixed by the recurrent representation. Section 4.3 uses this difference to state the separation from CoT in the compressed-memory regime.

4.3 Separation from chain-of-thought

The small-space simulation now gives the separation. A compressed loop whose persistent state is polylogarithmic, run for at most quasi-polynomially many steps, is a polylogarithmic-space machine. A chain-of-thought scratchpad grows in a different way. Each generated token is written into the context and remains available to later steps. Combining this space bound with standard expressivity results for polynomial-length CoT (Li et al., 2024; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024) yields a conditional separation on 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete serial tasks. The formal proof is in Appendix E.

Theorem 4.4 (Compressed-loop/chain-of-thought separation).

Assume 𝖯⊈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{P}\not\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), and let ℒ\mathcal{L} be 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete under logspace reductions. No logspace-uniform compressed-loop family with

s​d​p=polylog⁡(n),log⁡T=polylog⁡(n)s\,d\,p=\mathrm{polylog}(n),\qquad\log T=\mathrm{polylog}(n)

decides ℒ\mathcal{L}. By contrast, under standard chain-of-thought expressivity results, ℒ\mathcal{L} is decidable by a chain-of-thought family with polynomially many generated tokens.

Proof intuition. By Theorem 4.2, a compressed loop with s​d​p=polylog⁡(n)s\,d\,p=\mathrm{polylog}(n) and log⁡T=polylog⁡(n)\log T=\mathrm{polylog}(n) lies in 𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n). If such a loop decided a 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete language, then every language in 𝖯\mathsf{P} would be decidable in polylogarithmic space, contradicting the assumption. CoT is not subject to this compressed-state bound: its scratchpad grows as tokens are generated, and polynomial-length scratchpads reach the polynomial-time regime under the standard expressivity results (Li et al., 2024; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024). The full proof is in Appendix E.

The theorem addresses the compressed-state endpoint. The memory-rich endpoint has a different budget, since sequence-state loops carry n​d​pn\,d\,p persistent bits. This is the setting of the formal latent-thought comparison of Xu and Sato (2026), where looped or latent thought can outperform CoT on parallel-evaluable computations. The two conclusions therefore apply to different persistent-state budgets.

5 Empirical studies

The space bound suggests a concrete diagnostic. In a compressed loop, extra iterations let the model revisit the input and refine the same recurrent state, but they add no new places to store independent pieces of information. If this accounting carries over to trained finite models, then a task whose working-memory load can be dialled up should show a state-budget transition, with more persistent state helping as the load grows and added recurrence failing to relieve an undersized-state bottleneck.

We study two controlled settings in which the task load and the persistent-state budget vary independently. In pointer chasing the load is the number of independent chains tracked to a single final decode, and the budget is the number of compressed slots; in associative recall the load is the number of key-value pairs, and the budget is the recurrent state dimension. Both are finite-size probes of that prediction, with recurrence depth and training budget held fixed so that only the state knob varies. All seed-level numbers behind the two sweeps, with no run excluded from any reported aggregate, are tabulated in Appendix F.

5.1 A controlled slot sweep

Pointer chasing varies concurrent working-memory demand directly, with the number of compressed slots ss as the persistent-memory knob we sweep. The task is parameterised by kk, the number of independent pointer chains whose states must be maintained at once. Each instance gives a functional graph on n=16n=16 cells, kk start cells, and asks for the cell each chain reaches after a fixed number of hops. Under the single-final-decode protocol used here, a direct concurrent algorithm stores all kk current chain states at once, Θ⁡(k​log⁡n)\Theta(k\log n) bits; the experiment tests whether the compressed slots behave like such concurrent working memory. We compare compressed latent loops CLL⁡[s]\mathrm{CLL}[s] with ss persistent slots against a sequence-state loop (SSL\mathrm{SSL}, M=Θ⁡(n)M=\Theta(n)) control, sweeping s∈{1,2,4,8,16}s\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} and k∈{1,2,4,8}k\in\{1,2,4,8\}, T=16T=16 iterations, ten seeds. Both models instantiate the reasoners of Section 3. The compressed loop carries only its ss slots across the iterations, attending at each step to a cell table that is recomputed from the read-only input and never updated, so its persistent budget is MCLL=s​d​pM_{\mathrm{CLL}}=s\,d\,p in the sense of Definition 3.1, and each chain is read out by a query against the slots after the final iteration. The sequence-state control instead updates a hidden vector at all nn cells, matching Definition 3.2.

The finite-size prediction is deliberately one-sided. When the persistent state falls below the task’s concurrent-state demand, recurrence alone cannot repair the bottleneck, while sufficient nominal state does not by itself guarantee that training finds a solution. The slot count ss is a register-count bottleneck for the kk chains, so the subdiagonal regime s<ks<k is the stress test. In this experiment ss should be read as a register count, not a literal bit budget. Formally, s<ks<k is a bit-space lower bound only when d​p=Θ⁡(log⁡n)d\,p=\Theta(\log n) and each slot holds O⁡(1)O(1) chain states, whereas here n=16n=16 makes log⁡n\log n small relative to d​pd\,p. The theory does not assert a trainable threshold at s=ks=k; its converse (Lemma E.1) is conditional on sufficient iteration, routing, and trainability.

Figure 1 shows the 10-seed sweep. In the subdiagonal regime s<ks<k the collapse is robust, with mean cell accuracy 0.0410.041 and maximum cell-mean 0.1290.129. The collapse is also low-variance in the genuinely subcritical cells, with standard deviations between 0.000.00 and 0.020.02 for k∈{2,4,8}k\in\{2,4,8\} below the diagonal, so the failure below the slot budget is not a seed accident. The sequence-state control is essentially saturated, reaching 0.9990.999 mean accuracy for k=2,4,8k=2,4,8; at k=1k=1, nine of ten SSL\mathrm{SSL} seeds reach ≈1.00\approx 1.00 while one fails to train, giving a mean of 0.9360.936. We therefore treat the SSL\mathrm{SSL} result as a saturated control up to a single optimisation outlier.

The 10-seed sweep also shows that the above-threshold regime is not smooth. Some cells are reliably solved (k=2k{=}2 with s≥2s\geq 2, k=4k{=}4 with s∈{4,8}s\in\{4,8\}), but others are seed-dependent: for k=1,s=1k{=}1,s{=}1 the runs split into six high seeds and four low seeds with little mass between them, and the over-provisioned s=16s{=}16 column is unstable, with k=8,s=16k{=}8,s{=}16 ranging from near failure to near-perfect accuracy. These high-variance cells look less like noisy estimates of a single mean and more like mixtures of successful and failed training runs. Our interpretation is that, once the hard memory bottleneck is removed, the remaining failures are mostly about whether training finds a usable routing scheme, not a contradiction of the lower-bound direction. It is the same phenomenon as the router-initialisation trap of Sapunov (2026), where above the memory threshold success still depends on finding the right recurrent routing solution.

5.2 Associative recall with finite recurrent state

As a second controlled check, and following the recall-memory literature on efficient attention (Arora et al., 2024a; Arora et al., 2024b), we test the same memory-budget prediction in an associative-recall setting. Each example contains NN key-value associations, and the model must retrieve the correct value from a query. We vary the state dimension mm, so the recurrent state size is proportional to m​dm\,d for fixed width dd, in a gated linear-attention model; full softmax attention serves as a memory-rich control, and vanilla linear attention as a compressed-state negative control. For each seed and association load NN, let mcritm_{\mathrm{crit}} be the smallest state dimension mm whose accuracy reaches 0.90.9.

The result is a state-dimension crossover (Figure 2). The five-seed mean accuracy increases monotonically with mm for each association load NN, and the transition shifts to larger mm as NN increases. Full softmax attention is essentially saturated in every setting. Vanilla linear attention, even taking the best mm in the sweep, solves only the smallest association load and remains low for larger loads. As in the pointer-chasing sweep, the saturated and failed cells are stable across seeds, whereas transition cells show seed-dependent success/failure behaviour. We therefore report mcritm_{\mathrm{crit}} as a range across seeds rather than a sharp threshold: N=8N{=}8 has median 88 and range 44 to 1616, N=16N{=}16 has median 3232 and range 1616 to 6464, and N=24N{=}24 has median 6464 and range 3232 to 128128.

6 Discussion and limitations

The separation suggests a simple design principle. Test-time recurrence should be specified together with the state that persists across recurrences. A loop whose state is compressed can spend more time refining the same memory, but it does not acquire the growing scratchpad that CoT obtains by writing tokens. Full sequence-state loops and padded latent-thought constructions sit in a different regime, because their recurrent state scales with the sequence length or with added scratch positions. Persistent memory is therefore a resource of test-time compute alongside depth, width, and generated-token length.

For practical looped language models (Zhu et al., 2025; Jeddi et al., 2026), this separates two notions of memory efficiency. Sharing a key-value (KV) cache across loop depth, as in Conchello Vendrell et al. (2026), decouples memory from the number of recurrent iterations, but it does not by itself make the persistent state small relative to the input or context length. The compressed-loop bound applies most directly to models whose recurrent state is capped, pooled, low-rank, or otherwise sublinear in context length. A concrete experimental target is to expose the persistent-state budget as a controllable knob (the number of memory tokens, recurrent slots, state dimension, or cache rank) and measure how the critical budget scales with task load. The pointer-chasing and associative-recall sweeps in Section 5 are small examples of this type of measurement. Concurrent empirical work on adaptive looping and gated memory banks (Frey et al., 2026) asks a related architectural question, whether a looped Transformer should refine its hidden state for longer or add explicit learned storage; our separation isolates a complementary resource, the mutable activation state that persists across recurrences.

The experiments also point to an optimisation question. Once the state budget is large enough, success is not automatic, as threshold cells can be seed-dependent and over-provisioned memory can make routing unstable. Future work should separate capacity from trainability by measuring not only whether a state budget is sufficient in principle, but how reliably a model learns to use that state. Mechanistic analyses of routing, halting, memory-token specialisation, and recurrent fixed points (Blayney et al., 2026) would make this account more predictive.

Limitations and next steps.

The formal separation is asymptotic and conditional. It relies on the standard assumption 𝖯⊈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{P}\not\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), the log-precision, logspace-uniform model, and a compressed-loop definition in which the persistent recurrent state is capped independently of the input length. It does not lower-bound full sequence-state loops, loops with appended scratch positions, stochastic decoding, or architectures whose persistent state grows with the context. The experiments are finite-size probes of the state-budget effect rather than tests of the asymptotic theorem, and they do not prove task-level lower bounds for Sudoku, pointer chasing, or associative recall. A natural next step is to prove lower bounds for explicit task families and to scale the controlled experiments until the bit-level memory regime itself becomes active; the intermediate budgets between the s​d​ps\,d\,p compressed and n​d​pn\,d\,p sequence-state regimes, where many practical looped language models sit, are the most relevant targets.

The point, then, is to separate the resources these interfaces provide, not to rank looped Transformers against chain-of-thought. Recurrence, generated tokens, and full sequence state are different ways of buying test-time computation, but they buy different resources. Depth determines how many updates a model can perform; persistent memory determines what those updates can continue to remember. Any comparison of test-time reasoning interfaces should therefore specify both the computation performed and the state preserved across steps.

Appendix A Computational conventions

All results use the following standard conventions.

  • •

    The input x∈Σnx\in\Sigma^{n} is on a read-only tape addressed by an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-bit register; only the read/write work tape counts toward space.

  • •

    Activations are pp-bit fixed-point numbers in ℱp={a 2−p:a∈ℤ,|a|≤22​p}\mathcal{F}_{p}=\{a\,2^{-p}:a\in\mathbb{Z},\ |a|\leq 2^{2p}\}, so each uses Θ⁡(p)\Theta(p) bits, and we work in the log-precision regime p=O⁡(log⁡n)p=O(\log n) (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2023).

  • •

    Arithmetic, softmax exponentials, and reciprocals are deterministic pp-bit operations computed by specified logspace-uniform circuits, so the simulator reproduces the finite-precision block exactly with no approximation gap. In full generality the space bounds carry an additive poly⁡(p)\mathrm{poly}(p) term, still polylogarithmic under p=O⁡(log⁡n)p=O(\log n); the sharper O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)O(s\,d\,p+\log n) one-step bound of Lemma 4.1 assumes O⁡(p)O(p)-space arithmetic.

  • •

    A block BθB_{\theta} is a constant-size composition of multi-head attention and MLP sublayers with logspace-uniform weights (each weight bit computable from its index in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) space).

The three reasoners are those of Definitions 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3. For language recognition, a family decides L⊆Σ∗L\subseteq\Sigma^{*} if a fixed threshold on the decoder output equals 𝟙{x∈L}\mathbbm{1}_{\{x\in L\}} for every input xx.

Appendix B Proof of Lemma 4.1

Lemma 4.1 (One compressed-loop update in small space). Under the log-precision, logspace-uniform regime, one update z↦Bθ​(z,x)z\mapsto B_{\theta}(z\,;\,x) of a CLL⁡[s,d,p,T]\mathrm{CLL}[s,d,p,T] is computable in deterministic work-space O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)O(s\,d\,p+\log n), given zz stored on the work tape and xx on a read-only input tape.

Proof.

The update z↦Bθ​(z,x)z\mapsto B_{\theta}(z\,;\,x) is a constant-depth composition of attention and MLP sublayers; it suffices to bound one attention sublayer, since the constantly many sublayers reuse the same scratch and add only a constant factor. Fix a query slot j∈[s]j\in[s] and a head h∈[H]h\in[H] with head dimension dh=d/Hd_{h}=d/H.

Query. The query qj,h=WQ,h​norm​(zj)∈ℱpdhq_{j,h}=W_{Q,h}\,\mathrm{norm}(z_{j})\in\mathcal{F}_{p}^{d_{h}} is a fixed linear map of the slot vector zjz_{j} (d​pdp bits, on the work tape), computable in O⁡(d​p)O(dp) space.

Streaming the softmax readout. Let 𝒦=[n]⊔[s]\mathcal{K}=[n]\sqcup[s] index the nn read-only input keys and the ss old-slot keys. For u∈𝒦u\in\mathcal{K} let ku,vuk_{u},v_{u} be the corresponding finite-precision key and value: for an input position they are logspace-computable from xix_{i}, the position, and the parameters; for a slot position they are read from the stored old-slot buffer (Definition 3.1). The readout is

outj,h=∑u∈𝒦αu​vu,αu=exp⁡(ℓu−m)∑u′∈𝒦exp⁡(ℓu′−m),ℓu=⟨qj,h,ku⟩dh,\mathrm{out}_{j,h}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{K}}\alpha_{u}\,v_{u},\qquad\alpha_{u}=\frac{\exp(\ell_{u}-m)}{\sum_{u^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}}\exp(\ell_{u^{\prime}}-m)},\quad\ell_{u}=\frac{\langle q_{j,h},k_{u}\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{h}}},

with m=maxu∈𝒦⁡ℓum=\max_{u\in\mathcal{K}}\ell_{u}. Finite-precision addition is not associative, so we fix a deterministic summation order, by increasing index over 𝒦\mathcal{K}, using the same rounded fixed-point addition as the block; the block’s attention sums are defined in this order, so the simulator reproduces them exactly. We compute the readout in three read-only passes over 𝒦\mathcal{K}, storing no per-key quantity:

  • •

    Pass 1 computes m=maxu∈𝒦⁡ℓum=\max_{u\in\mathcal{K}}\ell_{u}: for each uu read its source (an input token xix_{i} via the O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-bit address register, or a stored slot), form kuk_{u} in O⁡(d​p)O(dp) space, compute ℓu\ell_{u} from qj,hq_{j,h} and kuk_{u}, and update the running maximum.

  • •

    Pass 2 computes Z=∑u∈𝒦exp⁡(ℓu−m)Z=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{K}}\exp(\ell_{u}-m) in the fixed order, recomputing each ℓu\ell_{u}, in one register holding a sum of up to n+sn+s terms in [0,1][0,1]; this fits in O⁡(p+log⁡(n+s))O(p+\log(n+s)) bits, absorbed by O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)O(sdp+\log n).

  • •

    Pass 3 accumulates outj,h\mathrm{out}_{j,h} into a dhd_{h}-dimensional ℱp\mathcal{F}_{p} register (O⁡(dh​p)O(d_{h}p) bits): for each uu recompute ℓu\ell_{u} (not stored), form αu=exp⁡(ℓu−m)/Z\alpha_{u}=\exp(\ell_{u}-m)/Z, and add αu​vu\alpha_{u}v_{u} in the same order.

Each pass uses O⁡(d​p+log⁡n)O(dp+\log n) work-space and reuses it across keys; the number of passes affects time but not space. Finishing all HH heads of slot jj and concatenating gives outj∈ℱpd\mathrm{out}_{j}\in\mathcal{F}_{p}^{d} in O⁡(d​p+log⁡n)O(dp+\log n) reused scratch.

Residual, MLP, write-back. The residual add and the width-dd MLP are a fixed circuit on the O⁡(d​p)O(dp)-bit vector, computable in O⁡(d​p)O(dp) space; the result is written to slot jj of a new buffer.

Synchronous update and aggregate. Because a sublayer may include slot-to-slot attention, each output slot must be computed from the old slot values. We therefore keep two s​d​ps\,d\,p-bit buffers, zoldz^{\mathrm{old}} and znewz^{\mathrm{new}}: every output slot is written into znewz^{\mathrm{new}} while all slot reads draw from zoldz^{\mathrm{old}}, and the buffers are swapped after the sublayer (matching the zcur/znewz^{\mathrm{cur}}/z^{\mathrm{new}} regions of Appendix C). This costs 2​s​d​p=O⁡(s​d​p)2sdp=O(sdp) persistent space; the per-slot scratch (O⁡(d​p+log⁡n)O(dp+\log n)) is reused across the ss slots, so the total work-space is O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)O(s\,d\,p+\log n).

Precision. Every quantity is computed to precision pp, matching the block’s definition, so the simulation outputs exactly Bθ​(z,x)B_{\theta}(z\,;\,x); there is no accumulated approximation error to control. ∎

Appendix C Proof of Theorem 4.2

Theorem 4.2 (Compressed loops are space-bounded). For any CLL⁡[s,d,p,T]\mathrm{CLL}[s,d,p,T] in the log-precision logspace-uniform regime, CLL⁡[s,d,p,T]⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n+log⁡T))\mathrm{CLL}[s,d,p,T]\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(O(s\,d\,p+\log n+\log T)). In particular, if s​d​p=polylog⁡(n)s\,d\,p=\mathrm{polylog}(n) and log⁡T=polylog⁡(n)\log T=\mathrm{polylog}(n), then CLL⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathrm{CLL}\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n).

Proof.

The simulator keeps two s​d​ps\,d\,p-bit regions zcur,znewz^{\mathrm{cur}},z^{\mathrm{new}} and a counter tt of ⌈log⁡T⌉\lceil\log T\rceil bits. It writes the seed z0=initθ​(x)z_{0}=\mathrm{init}_{\theta}(x) into zcurz^{\mathrm{cur}} (the initialiser, computable in O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)O(sdp+\log n) space). For t=0,…,T−1t=0,\dots,T-1 it computes znew=Bθ​(zcur,x)z^{\mathrm{new}}=B_{\theta}(z^{\mathrm{cur}}\,;\,x) by Lemma 4.1 in O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)O(sdp+\log n) space, copies znewz^{\mathrm{new}} over zcurz^{\mathrm{cur}}, and increments tt. After TT steps it applies the decoder to zcurz^{\mathrm{cur}} (O⁡(s​d​p)O(sdp) space) and thresholds. The input tape is re-scanned each iteration and is free. Work-space is reused across iterations, so the total is

O⁡(s​d​p)+O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n)+O⁡(log⁡T)=O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n+log⁡T).O(s\,d\,p)+O(s\,d\,p+\log n)+O(\log T)=O(s\,d\,p+\log n+\log T).

Thus the decided language lies in 𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(s​d​p+log⁡n+log⁡T))\mathsf{DSPACE}(O(sdp+\log n+\log T)). For s​d​p=polylog⁡(n)s\,d\,p=\mathrm{polylog}(n) and log⁡T=polylog⁡(n)\log T=\mathrm{polylog}(n), in particular for T=poly⁡(n)T=\mathrm{poly}(n), this is 𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n). With general pp-bit arithmetic the bound gains an additive poly⁡(p)\mathrm{poly}(p) term, still polylogarithmic under p=O⁡(log⁡n)p=O(\log n) (Appendix A). ∎

Appendix D Proof of Proposition 4.3

Proposition 4.3 (Sequence-state loops are memory-rich). For SSL⁡[d,p,T]\mathrm{SSL}[d,p,T] the persistent memory is MSSL=n​d​pM_{\mathrm{SSL}}=n\,d\,p, and SSL⁡[d,p,T]⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(n​d​p+log⁡n+log⁡T))\mathrm{SSL}[d,p,T]\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(O(n\,d\,p+\log n+\log T)), linear in the sequence length for fixed d,pd,p. Moreover, under 𝖯⊈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{P}\not\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), the class of sequence-state loop families with polynomially many positions is not contained in 𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n).

Proof.

For SSL⁡[d,p,T]\mathrm{SSL}[d,p,T] the persistent state is the full hidden sequence Ht∈ℱpd×nH_{t}\in\mathcal{F}_{p}^{d\times n}, of n​d​pn\,d\,p bits. Treating the nn positions as the slots of Theorem 4.2 gives SSL⁡[d,p,T]⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(n​d​p+log⁡n+log⁡T))\mathrm{SSL}[d,p,T]\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(O(ndp+\log n+\log T)), Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) for fixed d,pd,p. This O⁡(n​d​p)O(ndp) bound is memory-rich rather than tight: we do not claim every SSL\mathrm{SSL} needs linear space, but establish a class-level lower bound by importing two constructions. Giannou et al. (2023) realise an SSL\mathrm{SSL} that executes an arbitrary instruction stream encoded in the input, and Saunshi et al. (2025) show an SSL\mathrm{SSL} emulates a length-mm CoT by appending mm dummy positions, so that SSL\mathrm{SSL} with m=poly⁡(n)m=\mathrm{poly}(n) positions and T=poly⁡(n)T=\mathrm{poly}(n) iterations decides every language reached by polynomial-length CoT. By Li et al. (2024), polynomial-length CoT simulates polynomial-size Boolean circuits, and by Merrill and Sabharwal (2024), under their transformer-decoder assumptions polynomial-step CoT recognises exactly 𝖯\mathsf{P}; hence the languages reachable by polynomial-length CoT include all of 𝖯\mathsf{P}, in particular the 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete CVP. If SSL⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathrm{SSL}\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n) then CVP∈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathrm{CVP}\in\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), and since CVP is 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete under logspace reductions this would give 𝖯⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{P}\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), contradicting the hypothesis. Hence SSL⊈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathrm{SSL}\not\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n). ∎

Appendix E Proof of Theorem 4.4

We first bound a compressed loop’s space by its memory budget, which clarifies why iteration count alone does not suffice.

Lemma E.1 (Memory budget upper-bounds reachable space).

Write LOOP⁡[M]\mathrm{LOOP}[M] for a compressed loop with M=s​d​pM=s\,d\,p bits of persistent state, log-precision, and TT iterations. Then LOOP⁡[M]⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(M+log⁡n+log⁡T))\mathrm{LOOP}[M]\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(O(M+\log n+\log T)); for T=poly⁡(n)T=\mathrm{poly}(n) the counter costs log⁡T=O⁡(log⁡n)\log T=O(\log n) and the bound becomes 𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(O⁡(M+log⁡n))\mathsf{DSPACE}(O(M+\log n)).

Proof.

This is Theorem 4.2 with M=s​d​pM=sdp, the iteration counter staying within the same budget. ∎

Remark E.2 (Converse intuition).

Conversely, a deterministic computation using space w⁡(n)w(n) and halting within τ\tau steps can be represented by a LOOP⁡[M]\mathrm{LOOP}[M] with M=O⁡(w⁡(n))M=O(w(n)) and T=τT=\tau, provided the block realises the machine’s transition map. We use this only as intuition for why MM, rather than TT alone, is the governing resource; the separation below uses only the forward inclusion.

Theorem 4.4 (Compressed-loop/chain-of-thought separation). Assume 𝖯⊈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{P}\not\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), and let ℒ\mathcal{L} be 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete under logspace reductions. No logspace-uniform compressed-loop family with s​d​p=polylog⁡(n)s\,d\,p=\mathrm{polylog}(n) and log⁡T=polylog⁡(n)\log T=\mathrm{polylog}(n) decides ℒ\mathcal{L}; by contrast, under standard expressivity results ℒ\mathcal{L} is decidable by a chain-of-thought family with polynomially many generated tokens.

Proof.

For s​d​p=polylog​ns\,d\,p=\mathrm{polylog}n and log⁡T=polylog​n\log T=\mathrm{polylog}n, LOOP⁡[M]⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathrm{LOOP}[M]\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n) by Lemma E.1, the iteration counter staying within the same budget. Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete under logspace reductions. If such a compressed loop decided ℒ\mathcal{L}, then ℒ∈𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathcal{L}\in\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n). Every language in 𝖯\mathsf{P} reduces to ℒ\mathcal{L} by a logspace-computable reduction ff of polynomial output length, and the composition stays in polylogarithmic space, since each queried bit of f⁡(x)f(x) is recomputed in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) space and polylog⁡(|f⁡(x)|)=polylog⁡(n)\mathrm{polylog}(|f(x)|)=\mathrm{polylog}(n) as |f⁡(x)||f(x)| is polynomial in nn. Hence 𝖯⊆𝖣𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤⁡(polylog​n)\mathsf{P}\subseteq\mathsf{DSPACE}(\mathrm{polylog}n), contradicting the assumption. Under standard chain-of-thought expressivity results, polynomial-length CoT decides ℒ\mathcal{L}: Li et al. (2024) give the simulation of size-TT Boolean circuits by TT-step CoT, and Merrill and Sabharwal (2024) characterise the polynomial-step regime as exactly 𝖯\mathsf{P} under their model assumptions. Since ℒ∈𝖯\mathcal{L}\in\mathsf{P}, this gives the separation. ∎

Remark E.3 (Endpoints and the governing quantity).

More generally, by the forward inclusion of Lemma E.1 a language with deterministic space lower bound w⁡(n)w(n) cannot be decided by LOOP⁡[M]\mathrm{LOOP}[M] whenever M+log⁡n+log⁡T=o⁡(w⁡(n))M+\log n+\log T=o(w(n)); for poly⁡(n)\mathrm{poly}(n) iterations and w⁡(n)≫log⁡nw(n)\gg\log n this requires M=Ω⁡(w⁡(n))M=\Omega(w(n)), while CoT supplies Θ⁡(ℓ)\Theta(\ell) growing scratch and reaches such tasks at ℓ=poly⁡(n)\ell=\mathrm{poly}(n). The relative power is therefore governed by MM versus w⁡(n)w(n). At the memory-rich endpoint M=Θ⁡(n​d​p)M=\Theta(ndp) (Θ⁡(n)\Theta(n) for fixed d,pd,p), LOOP⁡[M]\mathrm{LOOP}[M] is the sequence-state loop, the latent-thought regime discussed in Section 2; our separation concerns the opposite, memory-constrained endpoint.

Appendix F Experimental details and seed-level results

This appendix reports the seed-level results underlying Figures 1 and 2. The tables are included only for reproducibility: every mean and standard deviation in Section 5 is computed over the listed seeds, with no failed, low, or outlier run excluded. Labels such as “failed seed”, “high seed”, and “low seed” are post-hoc descriptive terms for interpreting optimisation regimes, not filtering criteria.

Experimental setup.

Both sweeps train with Adam at learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, batch size 6464, for 12,00012{,}000 steps, and evaluate exact accuracy on 51205120 held-out examples (2020 batches of 256256). Pointer chasing uses functional graphs on n=16n=16 cells with 44-hop chains, hidden width d=64d=64, 44 attention heads, and T=16T=16 loop iterations; the compressed loop sweeps s∈{1,2,4,8,16}s\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} slots against k∈{1,2,4,8}k\in\{1,2,4,8\} chains, and an instance is correct only if all kk endpoints match. Associative recall uses inline multi-query associative recall with vocabulary K=64K=64, four queries per example, width d=128d=128 and four blocks, and a gated linear-attention block with a short causal depthwise convolution, sweeping state dimension m∈{4,8,16,32,64,128}m\in\{4,8,16,32,64,128\} against N∈{8,16,24}N\in\{8,16,24\} associations and scoring per-query-token accuracy.
